messages.content: You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

Please solve this issue: Our test suite grew big and we haven't noticed how the total RSpec run time outgrew 10 minutes (no parallelization) on CI.

We need to profile the test suite and identify the common problems (shared by many specs) and fix them once and for all. Keep refactoring of individual examples minimal: prefer configuration- and setup-level changes — adding tags, restructuring shared setup, wrapping execution. What the examples assert must stay the same. No app code changes affecting runtime behavior.

NOTE: Running the whole test suite is very time-consuming. Don't try to run the whole test suite (it would fail with timeout due to the Bash tool limitations) or even multiple directories. Only `rspec spec/<some-folder>`. Completely ignore system specs and streaming related specs (we do not run them by default anyway).

We will work on specific spec types at each optimization phase: `spec/models` and `spec/requests`. In the end, we want these two groups together to run at least twice as fast as they do today. Store any insights/comments/plans (such as baseline metrics) that could be useful for the future runs in the docs/ folder (so you can use that knowledge during future optimization runs).

Let's start with `spec/models`—don't touch other spec types during this step.
Also, do not touch factories yet — we will work on them later.

At least a 30-35% speed improvement for `spec/models` is expected; however, don't hesitate to squeeze more if you see an opportunity (aka low-hanging fruits).


You can execute bash commands and edit files to implement the necessary changes.

## Recommended Workflow

This workflow should be done step-by-step so that you can iterate on your changes and any possible problems.

1. Analyze the codebase by finding and reading relevant files
2. Create a script to reproduce the issue
3. Edit the source code to resolve the issue
4. Verify your fix works by running your script again
5. Test edge cases to ensure your fix is robust
6. Submit your changes and finish your work by issuing the following command: `echo COMPLETE_TASK_AND_SUBMIT_FINAL_OUTPUT`.

--require spec_helper
--- .simplecov ---
# frozen_string_literal: true

SimpleCov.configure do
  # During parallel runs, ensure unique names for post-run merge
  command_name "job-#{ENV['TEST_ENV_NUMBER']}" if ENV['TEST_ENV_NUMBER']

  if ENV['CI']
    require 'simplecov-lcov'
    formatter SimpleCov::Formatter::LcovFormatter
    formatter.config.report_with_single_file = true
  else
    formatter SimpleCov::Formatter::HTMLFormatter
  end

  enable_coverage :branch, :eval

  skip 'lib/linter'

  group 'Libraries', 'lib'
  group 'Policies', 'app/policies'
  group 'Presenters', 'app/presenters'
  group 'Search', 'app/chewy'
  group 'Serializers', 'app/serializers'
  group 'Services', 'app/services'
  group 'Validators', 'app/validators'
  group 'Views', 'app/views'
end
--- .env.test ---
# In test, compile the NodeJS code as if we are in production
NODE_ENV=production
# Federation
LOCAL_DOMAIN=cb6e6126.ngrok.io
LOCAL_HTTPS=true

# Secret values required by ActiveRecord encryption feature
# Use `bin/rails db:encryption:init` to generate fresh secrets
ACTIVE_RECORD_ENCRYPTION_DETERMINISTIC_KEY=test_determinist_key_DO_NOT_USE_IN_PRODUCTION
ACTIVE_RECORD_ENCRYPTION_KEY_DERIVATION_SALT=test_salt_DO_NOT_USE_IN_PRODUCTION
ACTIVE_RECORD_ENCRYPTION_PRIMARY_KEY=test_primary_key_DO_NOT_USE_IN_PRODUCTION
--- spec_helper.rb ---
# frozen_string_literal: true

if ENV.fetch('COVERAGE', false)
  require 'simplecov'
  SimpleCov.start 'rails'
end

RSpec.configure do |config|
  config.example_status_persistence_file_path = 'tmp/rspec/examples.txt'
  config.expect_with :rspec do |expectations|
    expectations.include_chain_clauses_in_custom_matcher_descriptions = true
  end

  config.disable_monkey_patching!

  config.mock_with :rspec do |mocks|
    mocks.verify_partial_doubles = true
  end

  config.before :suite do
    Rails.application.load_seed

# frozen_string_literal: true

module BrowserErrorsHelpers
  def ignore_js_error(error)
    @ignored_js_errors_for_spec << error
  end

  def error_message(error)
    error.keys.map { |key| "#{key.to_s.titleize}: #{error[key]}" }.join("\n")
  end
end

RSpec.configure do |config|
  config.include BrowserErrorsHelpers, :js, type: :system

  config.before(:each, :js, type: :system) do |example|
    @ignored_js_errors_for_spec = []

    example.metadata[:js_console_messages] ||= []
    Capybara.current_session.driver.with_playwright_page do |page|
      page.on('console', lambda { |msg|
        example.metadata[:js_console_messages] << { type: msg.type, text: msg.text, location: msg.location, page: msg.page.url }
      })
    end
  end

  config.after(:each, :js, type: :system) do |example|
    # Classes of intermittent ignorable errors
    ignored_errors = [
      /Error while trying to use the following icon from the Manifest/, # https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/pull/30793
      /Manifest: Line: 1, column: 1, Syntax error/, # Similar parsing/interruption issue as above
    ].concat(@ignored_js_errors_for_spec)

    errors = example.metadata[:js_console_messages].reject do |msg|
      ignored_errors.any? { |pattern| pattern.match(msg[:text]) }
    end

    if errors.present?
      aggregate_failures 'browser errrors' do
        errors.each do |error|
          expect(error[:type]).to_not eq('error'), error_message(error)
          next unless error[:type] == 'warning'

          warn 'WARN: browser warning'
          warn error[:text]
        end
      end
    end
  end
end

module BrowserErrorsHelpers
  def ignore_js_error(error)
    @ignored_js_errors_for_spec << error
  end

  def error_message(error)
    error.keys.map { |key| "#{key.to_s.titleize}: #{error[key]}" }.join("\n")
  end
end

RSpec.configure do |config|
  config.include BrowserErrorsHelpers, :js, type: :system

  config.before(:each, :js, type: :system) do |example|
    @ignored_js_errors_for_spec = []

    example.metadata[:js_console_messages] ||= []
    Capybara.current_session.driver.with_playwright_page do |page|
      page.on('console', lambda { |msg|
        example.metadata[:js_console_messages] << { type: msg.type, text: msg.text, location: msg.location, page: msg.page.url }
      })
    end
  end

  config.after(:each, :js, type: :system) do |example|
    # Classes of intermittent ignorable errors
    ignored_errors = [
      /Error while trying to use the following icon from the Manifest/, # https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/pull/30793
      /Manifest: Line: 1, column: 1, Syntax error/, # Similar parsing/interruption issue as above
    ].concat(@ignored_js_errors_for_spec)

    errors = example.metadata[:js_console_messages].reject do |msg|
      ignored_errors.any? { |pattern| pattern.match(msg[:text]) }
    end

    if errors.present?
      aggregate_failures 'browser errrors' do
        errors.each do |error|
          expect(error[:type]).to_not eq('error'), error_message(error)
          next unless error[:type] == 'warning'

          warn 'WARN: browser warning'
          warn error[:text]
        end
      end
    end
  end
end

module SignedRequestHelpers
  def get(path, headers: nil, sign_with: nil, **args)
    return super(path, headers: headers, **args) if sign_with.nil?

    headers ||= {}
    headers['Date'] = Time.now.utc.httpdate
    headers['Host'] = Rails.configuration.x.local_domain
    signed_headers = headers.merge('(request-target)' => "get #{path}").slice('(request-target)', 'Host', 'Date')

    keypair = sign_with.keypair
    key_id = keypair.uri
    signed_string = signed_headers.map { |key, value| "#{key.downcase}: #{value}" }.join("\n")

    signature = Base64.strict_encode64(private_key_from_keypair(keypair).sign(OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'), signed_string))

    headers['Signature'] = "keyId=\"#{key_id}\",algorithm=\"rsa-sha256\",headers=\"#{signed_headers.keys.join(' ').downcase}\",signature=\"#{signature}\""

    super(path, headers: headers, **args)
  end

  def post(path, headers: nil, sign_with: nil, **args)
    return super(path, headers: headers, **args) if sign_with.nil?

    headers ||= {}
    headers['Date'] = Time.now.utc.httpdate
    headers['Host'] = Rails.configuration.x.local_domain
    headers['Digest'] = "SHA-256=#{Digest::SHA256.base64digest(args[:params].to_s)}"

    signed_headers = headers.merge('(request-target)' => "post #{path}").slice('(request-target)', 'Host', 'Date', 'Digest')

    keypair = sign_with.keypair
    key_id = keypair.uri
    signed_string = signed_headers.map { |key, value| "#{key.downcase}: #{value}" }.join("\n")
    signature = Base64.strict_encode64(private_key_from_keypair(keypair).sign(OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'), signed_string))

    headers['Signature'] = "keyId=\"#{key_id}\",algorithm=\"rsa-sha256\",headers=\"#{signed_headers.keys.join(' ').downcase}\",signature=\"#{signature}\""

    super(path, headers: headers, **args)
  end
end

module SignedRequestHelpers
  def get(path, headers: nil, sign_with: nil, **args)
    return super(path, headers: headers, **args) if sign_with.nil?

    headers ||= {}
    headers['Date'] = Time.now.utc.httpdate
    headers['Host'] = Rails.configuration.x.local_domain
    signed_headers = headers.merge('(request-target)' => "get #{path}").slice('(request-target)', 'Host', 'Date')

    keypair = sign_with.keypair
    key_id = keypair.uri
    signed_string = signed_headers.map { |key, value| "#{key.downcase}: #{value}" }.join("\n")

    signature = Base64.strict_encode64(private_key_from_keypair(keypair).sign(OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'), signed_string))

    headers['Signature'] = "keyId=\"#{key_id}\",algorithm=\"rsa-sha256\",headers=\"#{signed_headers.keys.join(' ').downcase}\",signature=\"#{signature}\""

    super(path, headers: headers, **args)
  end

  def post(path, headers: nil, sign_with: nil, **args)
    return super(path, headers: headers, **args) if sign_with.nil?

    headers ||= {}
    headers['Date'] = Time.now.utc.httpdate
    headers['Host'] = Rails.configuration.x.local_domain
    headers['Digest'] = "SHA-256=#{Digest::SHA256.base64digest(args[:params].to_s)}"

    signed_headers = headers.merge('(request-target)' => "post #{path}").slice('(request-target)', 'Host', 'Date', 'Digest')

    keypair = sign_with.keypair
    key_id = keypair.uri
    signed_string = signed_headers.map { |key, value| "#{key.downcase}: #{value}" }.join("\n")
    signature = Base64.strict_encode64(private_key_from_keypair(keypair).sign(OpenSSL::Digest.new('SHA256'), signed_string))

    headers['Signature'] = "keyId=\"#{key_id}\",algorithm=\"rsa-sha256\",headers=\"#{signed_headers.keys.join(' ').downcase}\",signature=\"#{signature}\""

    super(path, headers: headers, **args)
  end
end

messages.thinking:
**Analyzing Performance Bottlenecks in the Test Suite**

Okay, hold on a second! This StackProf output from just a single file, `spec/models/trends/statuses_spec.rb`, is screaming at me! I need to dig deeper into why these performance issues are happening.

First, this `BCrypt::Engine.__bc_crypt` is taking up a whopping 2.7% of the samples, 243ms, and that's *just* for one fabricated user in this test! That's not right. I need to trace this call, figure out what's using BCrypt with such a high cost. Is it Doorkeeper? ActiveRecord's `has_secure_password`?  Is `ActiveModel::SecurePassword.min_cost` not set appropriately? Let's check the call chain.

Next, `ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#sql` is showing up big, 5.7% of samples, along with `IO#write` at 71 samples! Hold up, is the test environment writing every SQL query to `log/test.log`? Let's check `config/environments/test.rb`. Aha, `config.log_level` isn't set, meaning it defaults to `:debug`, and we're logging *everything*. Time to see how big that log file is becoming.

Now, this `ActiveSupport::Callbacks` thing at 66.9% of samples is even more worrying. What callbacks are being triggered? It's `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)`! Anytime a `Status`, `Bookmark`, or `Account` is created, it's enqueuing Sidekiq workers (`DistributionWorker`, `PushUpdateWorker`, etc.), and *because* `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)` is set globally in `rails_helper.rb`, all of those jobs are running synchronously. This is a massive overhead and the root cause.

Also, I'm noticing `Rails.application.load_seed` in `config.before :suite` - this runs *once* per rspec invocation, and isn't wrapped in a transaction! And what about those `config.after` blocks? `Rails.cache.clear` and `redis.del(redis.keys)` are running *after every single example*. That's 1,795 times!! We're doing unnecessary Redis calls, especially the `redis.del(redis.keys)` which is looping through keys. This is wasteful! We should be using `redis.flushdb` or only clear when Redis is used.

Also, the `config.before` block in `rails_helper.rb` reloading routes and doing more `Sidekiq.testing!(:inline)` calls...

But I'm not going to guess. We need concrete data. Let's profile the entire `spec/models` suite. I have `stackprof` and `test-prof` at my disposal. I'm going to run it using `TEST_STACK_PROF=1`, making sure the output format is manageable (probably text at first), to get a full, empirical picture of what's happening across all 1,795 examples. Time to dive deep.

        return unless profile

        end

        @locked = false
        @initialized = TestProf.require(

          MSG
          false
        end
      end

        html_path = path.gsub(/\.dump$/, ".html")

          stackprof --d3-flamegraph #{path} > #{html_path} && stackprof --flamegraph-viewer=#{html_path}
        MSG
      end

      def dump_json_report(path)
        report = ::StackProf::Report.new(
          Marshal.load(IO.binread(path))
        )
        json_path = path.gsub(/\.dump$/, ".json")
        File.write(json_path, JSON.generate(report.data))

        log :info, <<~MSG
          StackProf JSON report generated: #{json_path}
        MSG
      end
    end
  end
end

**My Immediate Concerns and Investigative Steps**

Oh. My. God! The numbers in StackProf total are *astounding*! I need to stop and really digest this. This is screaming for attention!

Looking at the lines within StackProf total, I'm seeing something truly alarming. `ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#sql` is consuming a staggering **32.5%** of the *entire* runtime of `spec/models`! Why is it taking up such a massive portion of the time? And right below that, the situation gets even worse.

`ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#log_query_source` is at **27.5%**, and `ActiveRecord::LogSubscriber#query_source_location` is at **26.8%**. This indicates a massive amount of time is being spent on logging database queries.

And then I look at StackProf self top 3:
- `String#sub`: **8.6%**
- `Thread::Backtrace::Location#to_s`: **5.0%**
- `Regexp#match?`: **3.8%**

Wait a second, do I see what's happening? Let's verify this!

The immediate question is...why are these logging methods running? Was `ActiveRecord.verbose_query_logs` enabled at some point, or is `log_query_source` the culprit? I need to check both the `/tmp/models_profile.txt` file (where I ran with `EVENT_PROF=sql.active_record`) AND the `config/` directory to make sure it's not enabled there.

Let's look at the baseline timing. Without `test-prof`, the `spec/models` suite took 152 seconds. With `test-prof` (StackProf + RSpecDissect + FactoryProf + EventProf) it jumped to 224 seconds. That's a huge slowdown!

The question is, was `verbose_query_logs` already enabled in `config/`, OR is it already running `spec/...` query source lines in `log/test.log`? I need to quickly examine the logs. I'll start with `tail -n 50 log/test.log` and also `grep -rn "verbose_query_logs" config/ spec/` to make sure! This is a priority!

messages.thinking:
**My Eureka Moment (and the Log File Disaster!)**

BINGO! BINGO! BINGO! Hold everything! I need to stop and take a close look at `log/test.log`. What's this madness in there by default, especially within the context of Rails 8.1? I'm seeing database queries from models like `EmailDomainBlock` and `UsernameBlock`, complete with their call stacks (look at those `↳ app/models/...` traces!). And then, `Rails.cache` reads and hits all over the place.

Wait a second. Why are these verbose query logs even in `log/test.log`? The `verbose_query_logs` setting is supposed to be limited to `development.rb`, right? Let me check `config/application.rb`. Ah-ha! In Rails 8, with `load_defaults 8.0` and onwards, or specifically, with `config/application.rb`, that `Rails.env.local?` is also set to `true` in `test`.

It's clear that from Rails 7.1+ / 8.0+, because of `Rails.env.local?`, it's writing an insane amount of data into `log/test.log`. Every single SQL query! And if `Rails.cache.logger = Rails.logger`, which could easily be set in something like `config/initializers/cache_logging.rb`, every cache read and write is logged, *too*. This means that every query is walking the entire Ruby call stack, formatting ANSI colors, and filtering parameters, and then writing a massive amount of data to `log/test.log` (78 MB in `spec/models` alone?!).

I need to see if any specs actually are testing `Rails.logger` in this repo. Let me inspect `config/application.rb` and do a quick search for `Rails.logger` in `spec/`.

I immediately need to understand *why*. Looking at `WebhookService`, it's clear: every single `after_create_commit` callback, across all `User`, `Status`, and `Report` models, is scheduling `TriggerWebhookWorker.perform_async`. This means every spec is re-fetching the objects from the database (`Account`, `Status`, `Report`), serializing the *entire* object graph (including all associated data via REST serializers, and dozens of SQL queries), only to throw away the result because the webhooks are disabled. **Analyzing Performance Bottlenecks in `spec/models`**

Okay, so looking at these performance metrics, my immediate thought is *wow*, the `TriggerWebhookWorker#perform` method is taking a massive chunk of time in `spec/models`, with 51,958 samples—that's 25.7% of the total! Meanwhile, `LocalNotificationWorker#perform` is practically a non-issue with a mere 165 samples. But hold on, the real head-scratcher is why `Sidekiq::Client#raw_push` shows such a high sample count: 54,160!

Digging deeper, it seems even when Sidekiq is in testing mode (either `:inline` or `:fake`), `Sidekiq::Client#raw_push` still involves `@redis_pool.with { |conn| conn.pipelined ... }`. Now, let's peek into `Sidekiq::Client#raw_push` in Sidekiq 8.1.6. It calls `conn.pipelined` even in test modes. In `:fake` mode, this results in the buffered Redis commands being pushed to an in-memory array via `Sidekiq::TestingClient#atomic_push` without the worker actually executing. So far, so good.

However, in `:inline` mode, `atomic_push` synchronously instantiates and executes `TriggerWebhookWorker#perform`, which explains the large sample count. This suggests a potential issue, especially considering `rspec-sidekiq` is probably in our Gemfile. I need to verify that `rspec-sidekiq` clears `Sidekiq::Worker.clear_all` before each example. Let's make sure! I should check if any spec in `spec/models` fails when `type: :model` is run with `Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)`.   last_webfingered_at   { Time.now.utc }
  public_key            { |attrs| attrs[:legacy_keypair] ? SigningKeysHelpers::PUBLIC_RSA_TEST_KEY : '' }
  private_key           { |attrs| attrs[:legacy_keypair] && attrs[:domain].nil? ? SigningKeysHelpers::PRIVATE_RSA_TEST_KEY : nil }
  suspended_at          { |attrs| attrs[:suspended] ? Time.now.utc : nil }
  silenced_at           { |attrs| attrs[:silenced] ? Time.now.utc : nil }
  requested_deletion_at { |attrs| attrs[:requested_deletion] ? Time.now.utc : nil }
  user                  { |attrs| attrs[:domain].nil? ? Fabricate.build(:user, account: nil) : nil }
  uri                   { |attrs| attrs[:domain].nil? ? nil : "https://#{attrs[:domain]}/users/#{attrs[:username]}" }
  discoverable          true
  indexable             true

  # This is not strictly needed but this avoids generating multiple keys
  # and, when `store_private_key` is passed, stores private keys for use in request specs
  keypairs do |attrs|
    if attrs[:legacy_keypair] || attrs[:public_key].present?
      []
    else
      [
        Keypair.new(
          type: :rsa,
          public_key: SigningKeysHelpers::PUBLIC_RSA_TEST_KEY,
          private_key: attrs[:domain].blank? ? SigningKeysHelpers::PRIVATE_RSA_TEST_KEY : nil,
          uri: attrs[:domain].nil? ? nil : "https://#{attrs[:domain]}/users/#{attrs[:username]}#main-key",
          local_fragment: attrs[:domain].nil? ? '#main-key' : nil
        ),
      ]
    end
  end
end

Thus, every single call to `Fabricate(:account)` ends up calling `BCrypt::Password.create`. This explains *perfectly* why we saw ~2,300 bcrypt calls instead of the expected 140. At 1.4ms per BCrypt call (due to that minimum cost of 4 enforced by `bcrypt-ruby` — even if we set `cost: 1`), this accounts for about 3.4 seconds of our runtime.

This underscores the significant impact of indiscriminate factory usage. And it also highlights the power of `let_it_be` and `before_all` in mitigating these issues.

      # Sidekiq::Batch is a Sidekiq::Pro feature. However the general consensus is
      # that, by default, you can't test without redis. RSpec::Sidekiq includes

      #       end

        attr_accessor :description
        attr_reader :bid

messages.thinking:
**Deep Dive into Test Performance: A Revealing Examination**

Okay, hold on a second! I just saw something in `app/models/setting.rb` that's got my mind racing! When I look at `app/models/setting.rb` side-by-side with `spec/spec_helper.rb`, the implications start to hit me.

First, I see that `spec_helper.rb` sets `Setting.registrations_mode = 'open'` before the specs even begin, using `Rails.application.load_seed`. Then, after *every single* example, `Rails.cache.clear` happens. This immediately raised a flag. Why? Because the `Setting` model is heavily cached. Every time a model like `User` or `Account` accesses settings, it checks `Rails.cache`. If the cache is missed, it hits the database with a query like `SELECT "settings".* FROM "settings" WHERE "settings"."var" = $1 LIMIT 1`. The `Rails.cache.clear` means those cache misses are likely to be *very* frequent.

Now I understand *why* `Rails.cache.clear` is there! The transactional nature of tests means that modifications to settings are rolled back, and the `after_commit :rewrite_cache` callback on `Setting` might not even fire. By clearing the cache, we ensure that stale data from the transaction doesn't persist. This is especially true if a test modifies the settings and it hasn't been cached before; `Rails.cache.fetch` caches the updated value, and if the cache is *not* cleared, that value stays stale in the cache even after the transaction rolls back. So clearing the cache *is* important for data integrity when dealing with any custom keys that are not ID-scoped, not just the default keys.

I'm thinking about performance. Is `Rails.cache.clear` slow? It’s only a microsecond to clear the memory store, but those database queries triggered by cache misses... how many are there per example? Probably only a few, specifically on tests that create a `User`, maybe 2-4 DB queries, around 0.3ms. Not huge, but it's multiplied across many examples. Clearing `Rails.cache` guarantees no cross-example cache pollution.

Now, let's look at Redis. I see `redis.del(redis.keys)` in `spec/rails_helper.rb`. This sends two commands to Redis. If we were to use `redis.flushdb` instead, we'd only need one. So, if we could track Redis usage during an example, we could avoid the `KEYS *` scan in many tests! If we add a `RedisClient` middleware that sets a thread-local variable `Thread.current[:redis_dirty] = true` on any write, then we can conditionally call `redis.flushdb` only if this flag is set. Then, for the majority of the model examples that do *not* touch Redis, we can eliminate unnecessary commands, leading to a huge reduction in network overhead. The vast majority of the time, the flag would be unused. That's a huge potential win! Even if the test does use Redis, the flushdb call is faster.

We need to check that nothing outside of Ruby is writing to Redis too. We know streaming specs use Node, but we can verify that everything is covered and still call the flushdb. This could eliminate thousands of unnecessary socket roundtrips.

---

Okay, now for something else: let's shift gears and look at the `Paperclip`, `Vips`, and `FFmpeg` integrations within `spec/models`. Based on a baseline profile, I see an example taking almost 3 seconds, specifically related to media attachments. It's time to dig into the test code to understand why. Examining `media_attachment_spec.rb`, along with related specs for avatars, headers, custom emojis, and preview cards, is crucial. It looks like it's time to deeply read the specs and see what’s going on.

              original: include(
                width: eq(fixture[:width]),
                height: eq(fixture[:height]),
                aspect: eq(fixture[:aspect])
              )
            )
        end
      end
    end
  end

  describe 'ogg with cover art' do
    let(:media) { Fabricate(:media_attachment, file: attachment_fixture('boop.ogg')) }
    let(:expected_media_duration) { 0.235102 }
    let(:expected_background_color) { '#268cd9' }

    it 'sets correct file metadata' do
      expect(media)
        .to have_attributes(
          type: eq('audio'),
          thumbnail: be_present,
          file_file_name: not_eq('boop.ogg')
        )

      expect(media_metadata)
        .to include(
          original: include(duration: be_within(0.05).of(expected_media_duration)),
          colors: include(background: eq(expected_background_color))
        )
    end
  end

  describe 'mp3 with large cover art' do
    let(:media) { Fabricate(:media_attachment, file: attachment_fixture('boop.mp3')) }
    let(:expected_media_duration) { 0.235102 }

    it 'detects file type and sets correct metadata' do
      expect(media)
        .to have_attributes(
          type: eq('audio'),
          thumbnail: be_present,
          file_file_name: not_eq('boop.mp3')
        )
      expect(media_metadata)
        .to include(
          original: include(duration: be_within(0.05).of(expected_media_duration))
        )
    end
  end

  it { is_expected.to validate_presence_of(:file) }

  describe 'size limit validation' do
    it 'rejects video files that are too large' do
      stub_const 'MediaAttachment::IMAGE_LIMIT', 100.megabytes
      stub_const 'MediaAttachment::VIDEO_LIMIT', 1.kilobyte
      expect { Fabricate(:media_attachment, file: attachment_fixture('attachment.webm')) }.to raise_error(ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid)
    end

    it 'accepts video files that are small enough' do
      stub_const 'MediaAttachment::IMAGE_LIMIT', 1.kilobyte
      stub_const 'MediaAttachment::VIDEO_LIMIT', 100.megabytes
      media = Fabricate(:media_attachment, file: attachment_fixture('attachment.webm'))
      expect(media.valid?).to be true
    end

    it 'rejects image files that are too large' do
      stub_const 'MediaAttachment::IMAGE_LIMIT', 1.kilobyte
      stub_const 'MediaAttachment::VIDEO_LIMIT', 100.megabytes
      expect { Fabricate(:media_attachment, file: attachment_fixture('attachment.jpg')) }.to raise_error(ActiveRecord::RecordInvalid)
    end

    it 'accepts image files that are small enough' do
      stub_const 'MediaAttachment::IMAGE_LIMIT', 100.megabytes
      stub_const 'MediaAttachment::VIDEO_LIMIT', 1.kilobyte
      media = Fabricate(:media_attachment, file: attachment_fixture('attachment.jpg'))
      expect(media.valid?).to be true
    end
  end

  describe 'cache deletion hooks' do
    let(:media) { Fabricate(:media_attachment) }

    before do
      allow(Rails.configuration.x.cache_buster).to receive(:enabled).and_return(true)
    end

    it 'queues CacheBusterWorker jobs' do
      Sidekiq.testing!(:fake)

      original_url = media.file.url(:original)
      small_url = media.file.url(:small)

      expect { media.destroy }
        .to enqueue_sidekiq_job(CacheBusterWorker).with(original_url)
        .and enqueue_sidekiq_job(CacheBusterWorker).with(small_url)
    end

    context 'with a missing remote attachment' do
      let(:media) { Fabricate(:media_attachment, remote_url: 'https://example.com/foo.png', file: nil) }

      it 'does not queue CacheBusterWorker jobs' do
        expect { media.destroy }
          .to_not enqueue_sidekiq_job(CacheBusterWorker)
      end
    end
  end

  describe '.combined_media_file_size' do
    subject { described_class.combined_media_file_size }

    it { is_expected.to be_an(Arel::Nodes::Grouping) }
  end

  private

  def media_metadata
    media.file.meta.deep_symbolize_keys
  end
end

def capture_emails(&block)
  if Sidekiq::Testing.fake?
    super do
      res = block.call
      Sidekiq::Queues['mailers'].dup.each do |job|
        Sidekiq::Queues['mailers'].delete(job)
        job['class'].constantize.new.perform(*job['args'])
      end
      res
    end
  else
    super
  end

# frozen_string_literal: true

module SidekiqMailerTestHelper
  def deliver_enqueued_emails(queue: nil, at: nil, &block)
    return super unless ActiveJob::Base.queue_adapter_name == 'sidekiq' && Sidekiq::Testing.fake?

    target_queue = (queue || ActionMailer::Base.deliver_later_queue_name || 'mailers').to_s
    before_jids = block ? Sidekiq::Queues[target_queue].to_set { |job| job['jid'] } : Set.new
    res = block&.call

    jobs = Sidekiq::Queues[target_queue].reject { |job| before_jids.include?(job['jid']) }
    jobs.each do |job|
      next if at && job['at'] && Time.at(job['at']) > at

      Sidekiq::Queues.delete_for(job['jid'], job['queue'], job['class'])
      Object.const_get(job['class']).process_job(job)
    end

    res
  end
end

**Analyzing the Performance Profile: Immediate Optimization Opportunities**

Okay, let's dive into this `/tmp/models_profile_2.txt` file. Finally, clarity! It's screaming at me where the bottlenecks are.

First, the big picture: the setup phase. It's taking a massive chunk of time, specifically, **80.4%** of the remaining time! The primary culprit? **`Fabricate.create` is consuming a staggering 77.7% of ALL remaining time** with 43,739 out of 56,274 samples. Clearly, Fabricators are the primary offender.

Diving deeper into the `STACKPROF SELF` numbers, here's the breakdown:

*   **Database Interactions:** `PG::Connection#exec_params`, `exec`, and `exec_prepared` are taking ~9.1 seconds, which is 16.3% of the time. This is almost entirely due to those repeated `let!` and `before` Fabrications.
*   **External Processes:** `IO.select` is burning **4.0 seconds (7.0%)** waiting on external `ffmpeg`/`ffprobe` subprocesses, which is from the `Terrapin::CommandLine` in Paperclip.
*   **BCrypt Overload:**  And here's the kicker: `BCrypt::Engine.__bc_crypt` takes **3.3 seconds (5.8%)**!

STOP! Let's pause on the `BCrypt` issue, this is something I need to fully understand. Now, I see the light. Looking at `Devise::Encryptor.digest` within `config/initializers/devise.rb`, the `config.stretches` variable is a clue. In the test environment, the cost is set to 1, while for production the cost is set to 10. `Devise::Encryptor.digest` calls `BCrypt::Password.create` which then calls `BCrypt::Engine.generate_salt(1)`. But the C extension minimum cost is 4! That means `bcrypt` is running `2^4 = 16` Blowfish key schedule rounds, which is roughly 1.4ms per call. The kicker? In `spec/models` (and even more so in `spec/requests`), `Devise::Encryptor.digest(klass, '123456789')` is being called **over 2,300 times** with the *exact* same password `'123456789'`! This is coming from the default Fabricator user (`Fabricator(:user)` -> `password '123456789'`).

Wait... if there are no app code changes affecting run-time behavior, then what about configuration in `spec/rails_helper.rb` or `spec/support/`? This raises a critical question: If a spec tests `user.valid_password?('123456789')` and another user, `user2`, also uses `user2.valid_password?('123456789')`, or if `user.valid_password?('wrong')` is called, does `Devise` care if two fabricated users share a memoized BCrypt hash for the same `(klass.pepper, klass.stretches, password)` in `Devise::Encryptor.digest`... unless a spec specifically asserts on salt uniqueness?! We need to check for that!

Right now, I'm going to grep the entire `spec/` directory for `encrypted_password` and `Encryptor`!

**Let's Deep Dive into `let_it_be` and Its Implications**

Okay, so I was just digging into `let_it_be.rb`, specifically lines 105-120, and some key insights are coming together.  First, the default modifiers are `{}`. That’s important to remember!  Then I saw that when you use `reload: true`, each time an example accesses that `let_it_be` variable for the *first* time, `record.reload` is invoked. This resets *all* the attributes and, crucially, clears any loaded association caches that might have been changed in previous examples.

Now, if we were to configure `TestProf::LetItBe.configure { |config| config.default_modifiers[:reload] = true }` – or use `reload: true` explicitly where records are being mutated within an example – a few things clicked. The performance cost of that `reload: true` is minimal, a mere `SELECT * FROM table WHERE id = $1 LIMIT 1`, roughly 0.08ms, which is nothing compared to the 35-130ms needed to `Fabricate` a record with its associations, validations, and callbacks.

What that `reload: true` buys us is *absolute* protection against Ruby in-memory mutations leaking across examples.  For instance, that means that updates like `alice.update(domain: 'example.com')` or cached associations like `account.bulk_imports.first` won't bleed into the next test! And even better: with `reload: true`, we're totally immune to `FrozenError` *and* memory leakage between examples. 

What about arrays of ActiveRecord objects, like `notifications`?  I looked at lines 209-215 of `let_it_be.rb`, and `reload` handles arrays too, calling `record.map { |rec| rec.reload }`. Although, for 8 read-only notifications, where we're only reading the `.id`, a plain `let_it_be` without `reload: true` does zero queries! So the smartest move seems to be keeping `let_it_be` standard – no surprises! – and using `reload: true` whenever an example mutates attributes or loads mutable associations on that shared record. That seems perfectly idiomatic with `test-prof`.

**Refactoring Test Setup for Efficiency and Clarity**

Okay, let's dive into some spec cleanup. I've been reviewing `spec/models/account_statuses_cleanup_policy_spec.rb`, `spec/models/tag_feed_spec.rb`, and `spec/models/public_feed_spec.rb`, and I see an opportunity for significant optimization, especially in reducing redundant setup code.

Specifically, in both `tag_feed_spec.rb` and `public_feed_spec.rb`, I've noticed the repetitive definition of `let(:viewer) { Fabricate(:account, username: 'viewer') }` within numerous nested contexts. This screams for refactoring. My plan is to leverage `let_it_be` to define these variables at a higher level, potentially using `reload: true` where necessary, such as `let_it_be(:user_viewer, reload: true) { Fabricate(:account, username: 'viewer') }` and `let_it_be(:moderator_viewer) { Fabricate(:moderator_user).account }`. This will streamline the setup and avoid unnecessary object instantiation.

In `public_feed_spec.rb`, lines 11-41 appear to rely on assertions like `include(...)` and `to_not include(...)` but don't seem to use `local_status` or `remote_status`. Lines 43-end define these same objects within their respective nested contexts. Even if the tests expect something to be empty, like in the `be_empty` tests, `local_status` and `remote_status` should *still* exist in the database and be filtered out. In `tag_feed_spec.rb`, lines 100-115, it's clear these are intentionally created to verify that disabled access is functioning correctly.

module Status::FetchRepliesConcern
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  # debounce fetching all replies to minimize DoS
  # Period to wait between fetching replies
  FETCH_REPLIES_COOLDOWN_MINUTES = 15.minutes
  # Period to wait after a post is first created before fetching its replies
  FETCH_REPLIES_INITIAL_WAIT_MINUTES = 5.minutes

  included do
    scope :created_recently, -> { where(created_at: FETCH_REPLIES_INITIAL_WAIT_MINUTES.ago..) }
    scope :not_created_recently, -> { where(created_at: ..FETCH_REPLIES_INITIAL_WAIT_MINUTES.ago) }
    scope :fetched_recently, -> { where(fetched_replies_at: FETCH_REPLIES_COOLDOWN_MINUTES.ago..) }
    scope :not_fetched_recently, -> { where(fetched_replies_at: [nil, ..FETCH_REPLIES_COOLDOWN_MINUTES.ago]) }

    scope :should_not_fetch_replies, -> { local.or(created_recently.or(fetched_recently)) }
    scope :should_fetch_replies, -> { remote.not_created_recently.not_fetched_recently }

    # statuses for which we won't receive update or deletion actions,
    # and should update when fetching replies
    # Status from an account which either
    # a) has only remote followers
    # b) has local follows that were created after the last update time, or
    # c) has no known followers
    scope :unsubscribed, lambda {
      remote.merge(
        Status.left_outer_joins(account: :followers).where.not(followers_accounts: { domain: nil })
              .or(where.not('follows.created_at < statuses.updated_at'))
              .or(where(follows: { id: nil }))
      )
    }
  end

  def should_fetch_replies?
    # we aren't brand new, and we haven't fetched replies since the debounce window
    !local? && distributable? && created_at <= FETCH_REPLIES_INITIAL_WAIT_MINUTES.ago && (
      fetched_replies_at.nil? || fetched_replies_at <= FETCH_REPLIES_COOLDOWN_MINUTES.ago
    )
  end
end

    scope :created_recently, -> { where(created_at: FETCH_REPLIES_INITIAL_WAIT_MINUTES.ago..) }
    scope :not_created_recently, -> { where(created_at: ..FETCH_REPLIES_INITIAL_WAIT_MINUTES.ago) }
    scope :fetched_recently, -> { where(fetched_replies_at: FETCH_REPLIES_COOLDOWN_MINUTES.ago..) }
    scope :not_fetched_recently, -> { where(fetched_replies_at: [nil, ..FETCH_REPLIES_COOLDOWN_MINUTES.ago]) }

    scope :should_not_fetch_replies, -> { local.or(created_recently.or(fetched_recently)) }
    scope :should_fetch_replies, -> { remote.not_created_recently.not_fetched_recently }

    # statuses for which we won't receive update or deletion actions,
    # and should update when fetching replies
    # Status from an account which either
    # a) has only remote followers
    # b) has local follows that were created after the last update time, or
    # c) has no known followers
    scope :unsubscribed, lambda {
      remote.merge(
        Status.left_outer_joins(account: :followers).where.not(followers_accounts: { domain: nil })
              .or(where.not('follows.created_at < statuses.updated_at'))
              .or(where(follows: { id: nil }))
      )
    }
  end

  def should_fetch_replies?
    # we aren't brand new, and we haven't fetched replies since the debounce window
    !local? && distributable? && created_at <= FETCH_REPLIES_INITIAL_WAIT_MINUTES.ago && (
      fetched_replies_at.nil? || fetched_replies_at <= FETCH_REPLIES_COOLDOWN_MINUTES.ago
    )
  end

That backtrace in `fetch_replies_concern_spec.rb` just slapped me in the face with the problem: an `ActiveRecord::RecordNotFound`! It turns out the issue lies in the lazy creation of `Account#account_stat`. Because `account.account_stat` is lazily created the *first* time a status or follow increments the counter on, for example, `alice`.

The problem? In Example 1, without `refind: true`, `Fabricate(:status, account: alice)` lazily creates the `AccountStat` within a savepoint transaction. Then it *caches* that `AccountStat` object in the Ruby memory as `@association_cache[:account_stat]` on `alice`. When Example 1 rolls back, it deletes `AccountStat` from Postgres, but `alice` in Ruby memory *still* holds the now-invalidated `AccountStat` in its `@association_cache[:account_stat]`!

The solution? `refind: true`! And, even better, by configuring `TestProf::LetItBe` with a default `refind: true` in `spec/rails_helper.rb`, like so:

1.  `refind: true` is intelligently targeted: *only* applies to `ActiveRecord::Base` objects (and arrays of them). It does a tiny PK lookup for each record in the array but can be avoided on an array if you pass `refind: false`.
2.  For any `let_it_be(:alice)` or `let_it_be(:account)` declaration, every example gets a *fresh* `Account.find(id)` (that's just 0.08ms!), with zero stale cache, instance variables, or mutated attributes.

require 'rails_helper'

RSpec.describe Form::CustomEmojiBatch do
  describe '#save' do
    subject { described_class.new({ current_account: account }.merge(options)) }

    let(:options) { {} }
    let(:account) { Fabricate(:admin_user).account }

    context 'with empty custom_emoji_ids' do
      let(:options) { { custom_emoji_ids: [] } }

      it 'does nothing if custom_emoji_ids is empty' do
        expect(subject.save).to be_nil
      end
    end

    describe 'the update action' do
      let(:custom_emoji) { Fabricate(:custom_emoji, category: Fabricate(:custom_emoji_category)) }
      let(:custom_emoji_category) { Fabricate(:custom_emoji_category) }

      context 'without anything to change' do
        let(:options) { { action: 'update' } }

        it 'silently exits without updating any custom emojis' do
          expect { subject.save }.to_not change(Admin::ActionLog, :count)
        end
      end

      context 'with a category_id' do
        let(:options) { { action: 'update', custom_emoji_ids: [custom_emoji.id], category_id: custom_emoji_category.id } }

        it 'updates the category of the emoji' do
          subject.save

          expect(custom_emoji.reload.category).to eq(custom_emoji_category)
        end
      end

      context 'with a category_name' do
        let(:options) { { action: 'update', custom_emoji_ids: [custom_emoji.id], category_name: custom_emoji_category.name } }

        it 'updates the category of the emoji' do
          subject.save

          expect(custom_emoji.reload.category).to eq(custom_emoji_category)
        end
      end
    end

    describe 'the list action' do
      let(:custom_emoji) { Fabricate(:custom_emoji, visible_in_picker: false) }
      let(:options) { { action: 'list', custom_emoji_ids: [custom_emoji.id] } }

      it 'updates the picker visibility of the emoji' do
        subject.save

        expect(custom_emoji.reload.visible_in_picker).to be(true)
      end
    end

    describe 'the unlist action' do
      let(:custom_emoji) { Fabricate(:custom_emoji, visible_in_picker: true) }
      let(:options) { { action: 'unlist', custom_emoji_ids: [custom_emoji.id] } }

      it 'updates the picker visibility of the emoji' do
        subject.save

        expect(custom_emoji.reload.visible_in_picker).to be(false)
      end
    end

    describe 'the enable action' do
      let(:custom_emoji) { Fabricate(:custom_emoji, disabled: true) }
      let(:options) { { action: 'enable', custom_emoji_ids: [custom_emoji.id] } }

      it 'updates the disabled value of the emoji' do
        subject.save

        expect(custom_emoji.reload).to_not be_disabled
      end
    end

    describe 'the disable action' do
      let(:custom_emoji) { Fabricate(:custom_emoji, visible_in_picker: false) }
      let(:options) { { action: 'disable', custom_emoji_ids: [custom_emoji.id] } }

      it 'updates the disabled value of the emoji' do
        subject.save

        expect(custom_emoji.reload).to be_disabled
      end
    end

    describe 'the copy action' do
      let(:custom_emoji) { Fabricate(:custom_emoji) }
      let(:options) { { action: 'copy', custom_emoji_ids: [custom_emoji.id] } }

      it 'makes a copy of the emoji' do
        expect { subject.save }
          .to change(CustomEmoji, :count).by(1)
      end
